en: Thus have I heard: the Ghoṭamukha Sutta, the ninety-fourth discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Venerable Udena was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Khemiyambavana.
Now at that time, the brahmin Ghoṭamukha had arrived at Bārāṇasī on some business.
Then, while walking and wandering for exercise, the brahmin Ghoṭamukha approached the Khemiyambavana.
Now at that time, the Venerable Udena was walking back and forth in the open air.
Then the brahmin Ghoṭamukha approached the Venerable Udena; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Udena.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he walked back and forth along with the Venerable Udena as he was walking, and said this:
“O ascetic, it is my view in this matter that ‘there is no righteous wandering life.
This is either because I have not seen those of such a nature, or because I do not know what the Dhamma in this regard is.”
When this was said, the Venerable Udena descended from his walk, entered the dwelling, and sat down on the prepared seat.
The brahmin Ghoṭamukha also descended from his walk, entered the dwelling, and stood to one side.
As the brahmin Ghoṭamukha was standing to one side, the Venerable Udena said this to him:
“There are seats available, brahmin.
If you wish, please sit down.
“Indeed, we were sitting here waiting for Master Udena.”
"How indeed could one such as I think it proper to sit on a seat without having been invited beforehand?
Then the brahmin Ghoṭamukha took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the brahmin Ghoṭamukha said this to the Venerable Udena:
“O ascetic, it is my conviction in this matter that ‘there is no righteous wandering life.
This is because I have not seen those of such a nature, or perhaps because of the doctrine [you preach] here.”
“But if you, brahmin, would grant what is worthy of being granted to me, and refute what is worthy of being refuted;
and if, regarding whatever I have said that you do not understand its meaning, you would ask me further about it:
‘Sir Udena, how is this? What is the meaning of this?’—only by doing so might there be a discussion between us on this matter.”
“I shall indeed grant permission to Master Udena where it is to be granted, and I shall reject what is to be rejected;

and as for whatever statement of Master Udena that I do not understand the meaning of, I shall question Master Udena further on that point: ‘How is this, Master Udena? What is the meaning of this? Thus...”
“Having done so, let there be a conversation and discussion between us on this matter.
“Brahmin, there are these four types of persons found existing in the world.
Which four?”
"Here, brahmin, a certain person is one who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment.
But here, brahmin, another person is one who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.

And here, brahmin, yet another person is both one who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and one who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others."

"But here, brahmin, there is a certain person who does not torment himself nor is devoted to the practice of torturing himself; he does not torment others nor is devoted to the practice of torturing others.
Being neither a tormentor of self nor a tormentor of others, in this very life he is free from hunger, extinguished, become cool, experiencing bliss, and dwells with a self that has become sublime.
Of these four types of persons, brahmin, which one satisfies your mind?"
“Master Udena, this person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment does not please my mind;
Master Udena, this person who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others also does not please my mind;

Master Udena, this person who both torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and who both torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others, also does not please my mind.”
But as for this person, Master Udena, who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment,
and who neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others— he, being neither a self-tormentor nor a tormentor of others,
is in this very life free from hunger, extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, and dwells with a self that has become sublime.
“This person alone wins my heart.
“But why, brahmin, do these three persons not win your heart?
“Because, Master Udena, that person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment torments and tortures himself—though he desires happiness and recoils from suffering;”
"This person does not please my mind. That person,
Master Udena, who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others— tormenting and burning others who desire happiness and loathe suffering—
does not please my mind."
"Master Udena, this person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment,
and who also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others— since he torments and afflicts both himself and others, who desire happiness and recoil from suffering,
this person does not satisfy my mind."
But as for this person, Master Udena, who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment,
and who neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others— he, being neither a self-tormentor nor a tormentor of others,
is in this very life free from hunger, extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, and dwells with a self that has become sublime; he [knows] both himself...
"Furthermore, one neither torments nor causes another who desires happiness and recoils from suffering to be tormented;
by this means, this person wins over my mind.
"Brāhmaṇa, there are these two assemblies."
Which two?
Here, brahmin, one assembly is passionately attached to jewels and earrings; it seeks children and wives, it seeks male and female slaves, it seeks fields and lands, and it seeks gold and silver.

But here, brahmin, another assembly is not passionately attached to jewels and earrings; having abandoned children and wives, having abandoned male and female slaves, having abandoned fields and lands, and having abandoned gold and silver, they have gone forth from the home life into homelessness.
"There is, brahmin, a person who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of torturing himself, and who neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of torturing others.
Neither tormenting himself nor tormenting others, he dwells in this very life free from hunger, extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, with his self become sublime.
In this regard, brahmin, which kind of person do you most often see belonging to which assembly?"
This assembly, which is passionately attached to jewels and earrings, seeks children and wives, seeks male and female slaves, seeks fields and lands,
and seeks gold and silver; and this assembly, which is free from such passion, having abandoned children and wives,
abandoned male and female slaves, abandoned fields and lands, and abandoned gold and silver—
“Having abandoned the home life for the homeless state?
“Sir Udena, that person who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment,
and neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others— he, not tormenting himself and not tormenting others, is in this very life free from hunger.”
Extinguished, become cool, experiencing bliss, he dwells with a self that has become sublime. This person, from this assembly—

those who have abandoned their passion for jewels and earrings, who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness, having renounced children and wife, male and female slaves, fields and lands, and gold and silver— I [regard him as such].
“I observe this frequently in this assembly.
[The Blessed One said: “But just now, brahmin, you said: ‘We understand it thus:
“O ascetic, there is no righteous wandering life;”’”
"This is how it appears to me here.
And that is either because I do not see those of other states of existence, or because of the nature of the phenomena involved.
"Surely, Master Udena, these words of mine were spoken with a firm conviction."
“There is a righteous wandering”—
this is how it appears to me in this matter.
And may Master Udena remember me thus.

“Those four types of persons who were mentioned in brief by the venerable Udena but not analyzed in detail—please, sir Udena, out of compassion for me, may you analyze these four types of persons in detail.
“In that case, brahmin, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, sir,” the brahmin Ghoṭamukha replied to the Venerable Udena.
The Venerable Udena said this:
“And what kind of person, brahmin, is one who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment?

Here, brahmin, a certain person goes naked, rejecting conventions, licking his hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked; he does not accept food brought to him, nor food specially prepared for him, nor an invitation.”
Thus, he does not accept from the mouth of a jar, nor from the mouth of a basket;

not with a sheep between, nor with a staff between, nor with a pestle between; not from two people eating together, nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman nursing, nor from a woman in her courses, nor from groups of people, nor where she is standing close by, nor where there are flies.
Moving from house to house, he eats neither fish nor meat, nor does he drink liquor, spirits, or fermented grain-liquor.
He is a "one-house" man or a "one-meal" man; or he is a "two-house" man or a "two-meal" man... up to... a "seven-house" man or a "seven-meal" man;
he subsists on a single alms-gift, or he subsists on two alms-gifts... up to... seven alms-gifts.
He takes food once a day, or he takes food once every two days... pe ...or he takes food once every seven days; thus he dwells devoted to the practice of taking meals at intervals up to half a month.

He becomes one who eats greens, or one who eats millet, or one who eats wild rice, or one who eats horse-gram, or one who eats hemp-seeds, or one who eats rice-powder, or one who eats the water from rinsing rice, or one who eats oil-cake.
Or he is one who eats grass, or one who eats cow dung, or he subsists on forest roots and fruits, eating only what ripens naturally.
He wears garments of hemp, or garments of flax, or shrouds from a cemetery, or rag-robes, or bark from the *tirīṭa* tree,
or antelope skins, or strips of antelope skin, or garments made of kusha grass.
He wears garments of bark, he wears garments of wood-shavings, he wears a blanket of human hair, he wears a blanket of animal hair,
or he wears an owl’s wing-feathers;
he is one who plucks out his hair and beard, devoted to the practice of plucking out his hair and beard.
He is one who stands continuously, rejecting seats;
he is one who squats, devoted to the exertion of squatting;
he is one who uses a bed of thorns, spreading his sleep upon a bed of thorns.
He dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water for a third time every evening—
thus he dwells devoted to various kinds of practices involving the mortification and tormenting of the body. This,
brahmin, is called the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment.
"And what, brahmin, is the person who torments others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others?

Here, brahmin, a certain person is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs, a fowler, a hunter, a trapper, a fisherman, a thief, an executioner, a butcher of cattle, a jailer—or anyone else engaged in cruel occupations.
This, brahmin, is called the person who torments others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others."
And who, brahmin, is the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others?
Here, brahmin, a certain person is either a head-anointed kshatriya king or a wealthy brahmin.
Having had a new assembly hall built to the east of the city, he shaves off his hair and beard and puts on a rough hide.

Having dressed himself and anointed his body with ghee and oil, he enters the new assembly hall together with his chief queen and the brahmin family priest, scratching his back with a deer horn. There,
he makes his bed upon the bare ground smeared with green cow dung.
Of a single cow that has calves of similar appearance, the milk from one udder sustains the king;
the milk from the second udder sustains the chief queen; the milk from the third udder sustains the brahmin family priest;
and the milk from the fourth udder he uses to offer oblations to the sacrificial fire.
With the remainder, he sustains a calf.
He speaks thus:
‘Let so many bulls be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice; let so many young bulls be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice; let so many...’
“Let so many heifers be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice; let so many goats be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice; let so many rams be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice;
let so many horses be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice; let so many trees be cut down for the sake of sacrificial posts;
let so much grass be mown for the sake of the sacrificial strew.”
Even those whom they call ‘slaves,’ ‘servants,’ or ‘laborers’ perform their tasks driven by the threat of punishment and the fear of danger, weeping with tearful faces.
This, brahmin, is called the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and who also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
And what, brahmin, is the person who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and who neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others?
How does one dwell, not tormenting oneself and not tormenting others, free from hunger, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, with self become Brahmā?

Here, Brahmin, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Thus, having realized this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.

He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, both in meaning and in phrasing; he reveals the holy life (brahmacariya) in its entirety, perfect and pure.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family, hears that Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.
Possessed of that attainment of faith, he reflects thus:
"Household life is crowded and dusty; going forth is the open air."
"It is not easy for one living in a household to lead the holy life in its complete perfection, in its total purity, polished like a conch shell.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Then, at a later time, having abandoned a small or a large mass of wealth, he went forth.

Having abandoned either a small circle of relatives or a large circle of relatives, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron-colored robes, he goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, having entered upon the training and way of life of the bhikkhus, he abandons the taking of life; from the taking of life...
He abstains from taking life; laying aside the rod and the sword, he dwells conscientious and compassionate, sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a heart free from theft.
Having abandoned unchastity, he lives a life of chastity; he dwells aloof, refraining from sexual intercourse, the common practice of the village.
Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks the truth, is devoted to truth, is trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech;

having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people from those, nor having heard something there, does he repeat it here for the purpose of dividing those people from these. Thus, he does not create division among those who are divided...

He is a reconciler of those who are divided or a provider of what is needed for those who are united; he delights in concord, rejoices in concord, finds joy in concord, and speaks words that bring about concord.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. He speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-stirring, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people. He speaks such words as these.

Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks on the Dhamma, speaks on the Vinaya; he utters speech that is worth treasuring, timely, reasoned, measured, and beneficial.
He abstains from damaging seeds and plants.
He eats only one meal a day, refraining from eating at night and abstaining from food outside the proper time.
He abstains from dancing, singing, instrumental music, and witnessing spectacles.
He abstains from wearing garlands, using perfumes and cosmetics, and adorning himself with ornaments.
He abstains from high and luxurious beds and seats.
He abstains from accepting gold and silver.
He abstains from accepting raw grain.
He abstains from accepting raw meat.
He abstains from accepting women and girls.
He abstains from accepting male and female slaves.
He abstains from accepting goats and sheep.
He abstains from accepting chickens and pigs;
he abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares;
he abstains from accepting fields and land.
He abstains from the practice of running messages and errands.
He abstains from buying and selling.
He abstains from cheating with false weights, false metals, and false measures.
He abstains from suborning, deceiving, cheating, and crooked practices.
He abstains from mutilating, murdering, binding, robbing, plundering, and using violence.
He is content with robes that suffice for his body and almsfood that suffice for his belly. Wherever he goes, he sets out taking only these with him.

Just as a winged bird, wherever it flies, flies burdened by its own wings, even so a bhikkhu is content with robes to protect the body and almsfood to sustain the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking these with him.
Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the happiness that is blameless.
Thus, having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with the eye faculty unguarded, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the eye faculty and achieves restraint over the eye faculty.
Having heard a sound with the ear … having smelled an odor with the nose … having tasted a flavor with the tongue …
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
If one dwells with this faculty of the mind unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—[might arise].
If unwholesome states were to flow into him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the faculty of the mind and attains mastery over the faculty of the mind.
Endowed with this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself an untainted happiness.
He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside.
He acts with clear comprehension when bending and extending his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl;
he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating;
and he acts with clear comprehension when going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
Thus, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, endowed with this noble contentment,
endowed with this noble restraint of the sense faculties, and endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension,
he resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Then, having returned from his almsround after the meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate toward all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind calmed within; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells as one who has crossed beyond doubt, free from uncertainty regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.
Thus, having abandoned these five hindrances— defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—
secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first *jhāna*, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought,

and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second *jhāna*, which is internal tranquility and singleness of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
With the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: “He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness,” and thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births... [and so on].
Forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births—
even many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, and many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion:
“In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;”
"Having passed away from there, I arose there; there I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
having passed away from there, I have reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma: "Alas, these beings..."

These worthy beings, possessed of misconduct of body... [and so on] ...revilers of the noble ones, holding wrong view, undertaking actions based on wrong view, have—upon the breakup of the body, after death—reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But these worthy beings, possessed of good conduct of body... [and so on] ...not revilers of the noble ones, holding right view...
‘...having undertaken actions based on right view, with the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a happy destination,
a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—
inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
He understands as it really is: “This is suffering”; he understands as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering”;
he understands as it really is: “This is the cessation of suffering”; he understands as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”
One understands things as they truly are:
one understands as it truly is, ‘These are the taints’; one understands as it truly is, ‘This is the origin of the taints’;
one understands as it truly is, ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; one understands as it truly is, ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’
He understands it as it truly is.
For one who knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When liberated, there arises the knowledge: "It is liberated."
‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.

This, brahmin, is called the person who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of torturing himself, and who neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of torturing others.
Neither tormenting himself nor tormenting others, he dwells in this very life free from hunger, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, having become one with the Brahmā-nature.”
When this was said, the brahmin Ghoṭamukha said to the Venerable Udena:
"Excellent, Master Udena! Excellent, Master Udena!
Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost..."
Or one who might show the way, or one who might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been elucidated by Master Udena in many ways.
I go for refuge to Master Udena, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May Master Udena accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
“Do not go to me for refuge, brahmin.
Go for refuge to that Blessed One to whom I have gone for refuge.”
“But where, Master Udena, does that Blessed One Gotama, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwell now?
“Brahmin, that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has now attained final Nibbāna.
“Even if we were to hear that Master Gotama was ten *yojanas* away, Master Udena, we would travel those ten *yojanas* to see that Master Gotama, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
Even if we were to hear of that Blessed One Gotama from twenty yojanas away… from thirty yojanas away… from forty yojanas away… [we would go].
"Even fifty yojanas, Master Udena, we would travel even fifty yojanas to see that Blessed Gotama, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Even if we were to hear of that Blessed Gotama from a hundred yojanas away, Master Udena, we would travel even a hundred yojanas to see that Blessed Gotama, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
"But since that venerable Gotama has attained final Nibbāna, Master Udena, we go for refuge even now to that venerable Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Udena accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
Furthermore, Master Udena, the King of Aṅga gives me a daily regular alms-offering; from that, I shall give one regular alms-offering to you, Master Udena."
“But, brahmin, does the King of Aṅga give you a regular daily alms-offering?
“Five hundred kahāpaṇas, Master Udena.
“Brahmin, it is not permissible for us to accept gold and silver.”
“If it does not suit you, Master Udena, I shall have a monastery built for Master Udena.
“If you wish to have a monastery built for me, brahmin, then have an assembly hall built for the Saṅgha in Pāṭaliputta.
“I am even more pleased and satisfied with this, Master Udena, that Master Udena encourages me to give to the Saṅgha.”
“Sir Udena, with this regular alms-offering and another regular alms-offering, I shall have a hall for the Saṅgha built in Pāṭaliputta.
Then the brahmin Ghoṭamukha, with that regular alms-offering and another regular alms-offering, had a hall for the Saṅgha built in Pāṭaliputta.
That is what is called today the “Ghoṭamukhī Hall.”
The Ghoṭamukhasutta is finished; it is the fourth.
